summaries.Q2843748: The only museum in the world devoted to Ingres, who was born in the town, it holds 4,500 of his drawings, the largest such collection in the world, 44 paintings and his violin. A whole floor is given over to Antoine Bourdelle, the town's other native son. On the eve of the Second World War, the Mona Lisa was brought here for safekeeping along with other works from the Louvre.
summaries.Q2942243: Built of white stone at the highest point of the town centre, in a town of red brick, it was ordered by Louis XIV after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, to assert Catholicism in a town won over to Protestantism. In 1707 six piers of the nave, built with badly fired bricks, collapsed and brought down part of the vault; consecration had to wait until 1739. Closed since 2020 because of cracks, it will reopen once strengthened.
summaries.Q3396779: Seven pointed arches pierced with high openings to let floodwaters through, and a flat deck, rare in the Middle Ages, over 205 metres: work began in 1311 on the orders of Philip the Fair and dragged on until about 1335, the town officials being accused of diverting the royal funds. Of the three towers planned, two were built, then demolished in 1663 and 1701. The Sainte-Catherine chapel, in the middle, disappeared in 1828.
summaries.Q3323271: The first major commission of Bourdelle, a son of the town: this memorial to the dead of the 1870 war moves from assault to combat to death, in bodies distorted beyond anything lifelike. The first model, too romantic, was badly received by the committee; it took Rodin's intervention, in 1897, for him to carry it out without compromise. On place de la Bourse in 1902, on place Bourdelle since 1970.
summaries.Q19366621: The Tarn can rise six metres in twelve hours: a structure as transparent as possible was needed. Simon Boussiron's design, chosen in 1910, splits the crossing into two reinforced concrete bridges, one with two spans of 53 and 56 metres over the river, the other a bow-string over the Lissac canal. Opened on 29 June 1913, it waited until January 1926 to see the tramway, which was stopped as early as the end of 1933.
summaries.Q3390010: The heart of the bastide, the square is lined with a double row of arcaded galleries that bore the names of the goods traded there: Wheat to the north, Cloth Merchants to the south, Fruit to the east, Clogs to the west. After the fire of 1614, the consuls imposed brick instead of wood and Louis XIII granted 16,000 livres; a second fire, in 1649, destroyed the north and the east. Everything was completed in 1713.
summaries.Q21294421: The rooms of the Black Prince's unfinished castle served for a century and a half as a hideout for thieves and courtesans, driven out in 1520 by the seneschal of Quercy. Louis XIV gave the ruined buildings to Bishop Pierre de Bertier, who had plans drawn up in 1664; he moved in in 1671 and died three years later in a carriage accident. Town hall after the Revolution, the palace today houses the musée Ingres-Bourdelle.
summaries.Q21294409: Commissioned from Antoine Bourdelle in August 1921, who presented several versions up to 1925, it takes the form of a columned temple sheltering the altar of the dead. In front, a bronze of victorious France looks to the horizon, that is, to the future; at her sides, a shield for Law and a serpent for intelligence. Unveiled on cours Foucault on 13 November 1932, eleven years after the commission.
summaries.Q23926744: Housed in the former Hôtel de la Cour des aides, a few steps from the Pont Vieux, the museum grew out of the pooling of the collections of a learned society in 1852. Its curator Victor Brun discovered, in May 1864, in the Aveyron valley, the "Dame de Bruniquel", a skeleton 15,300 years old. More than 2,500 mounted animals, among them the emblematic female elephant, a body given by the Pinder circus in 1894.
summaries.Q107414543: Built in 1865 in a neo-Renaissance style by Henri Bach, of Toulouse, it stands on the former Bishop's garden, a public promenade laid out in 1658. Following the law of 1905, the bishops left their palace in the town centre in 1909 and bought this château, where they lived until 1969. The Department acquired it in 1974 and built the present Hôtel du Département beside it. Louis Malle filmed Lacombe Lucien here.
summaries.Q3581867: Built in the 13th century shortly after the town was founded, it is the oldest historic monument in Montauban; with the Pont Vieux, one of the two medieval remains still in use. In 1561 the Calvinists brought down its vault and its spire, and the fortified base of the octagonal bell tower still bears the marks of cannonballs from the siege of 1621, led by Louis XIII. Richelieu ordered its rebuilding in 1629.
summaries.Q22940263: Built for the Carmelites in the spirit of the Counter-Reformation and consecrated in 1682, this brick building passed to Protestant worship at the Revolution: a Reformed merchant bought it in 1791, during the sale of Church property. The first service was held there on 20 January 1793, after the intervention of Jeanbon Saint-André, member of the Convention and a former pastor of the town. It still houses a parish of the United Protestant Church.
summaries.Q131106320: A U-shaped plan, rare in Montauban: two wings of unequal length, since rue Lasserre and the allées below are not parallel. The half-moon porch made it easier to manoeuvre carriages; the keystone of the gateway arch bears the head of a bearded man. To the right, a plaque recalls the part played by the Baron de Mortarieu, mayor under the Empire, in the creation of the Tarn-et-Garonne in 1808. The mansion is today privately owned flats.
summaries.Q2392062: Born of the gift, in 1975, of the collection of the rose grower Roger Sucret, opened in 1983 and named after François Mitterrand in 1998, it has held as many as 12,000 rose bushes and a thousand varieties, arranged by their 97 breeders. It occupies parc Chambord, so named in 1820 when it covered 20 hectares; the Ingréo aquatic centre pushed it back in 2013.
summaries.Q27339189: The Villebourbon district wore churches out: the one of 1650, built too close to the river, was swept away by the water two years later; the next, rebuilt further back and then enlarged, became too small and disappeared in its turn. The present neo-Gothic building dates from 1870-1891, and its bell tower was not finished until 1935.
summaries.Q106714892: Born of the meeting between a collector, Gérard Misrai, and a businesswoman who had empty premises, this private museum run by volunteers opened in December 2016. The toys are staged in scenes: lead soldiers in the middle of a battle, the Tour de France pack attacking a mountain pass. There is a Sagrada Familia made of Meccano, and one area lets you play pinball or table football.
